Biryar ships with the shops it has been able to read. Your supplier is
probably not one of them. This is how you add it.

An adapter is a class. It inherits from nothing, registers nothing, and
is handed a page of HTML and asked for offers. Everything else —
fetching, robots.txt, rate limiting, the scraping proxy, resuming where
the last pass stopped, the Keepa lookup, the screening against your own
measured Amazon fees — already exists and is not your problem.

## The loop

```bash
python -m biryar.adapters new mybookshop --country GB --domain mybookshop.co.uk
python -m biryar.adapters check mybookshop --url https://mybookshop.co.uk/some-product
```

`new` writes `adapters/mybookshop.py`: a working adapter for a shop that
publishes schema.org JSON-LD, which most do. Run `check` against one
real product page before you change anything — if the shop is
conventional you are already finished.

When it reads nothing, `check` tells you which of the two things went
wrong, because they need opposite responses:

```
Fetched https://mybookshop.co.uk/some-product
  ok 200 · 574,844 bytes

parse() returned nothing from this page.
```

That is a parser problem. This is not:

```
  http_error 403 · 0 bytes
```

Three modes, cheapest first:

| | What it does |
|---|---|
| `check <slug> --file saved.html --url <url>` | Reads a page off disk. No network, no scraping key, no database, no robots.txt. The loop for working on a parser. |
| `check <slug> --url <url>` | Fetches one page the way a scan does: robots.txt honoured, the retailer's delay, your scraping key if the adapter asks for one. |
| `check <slug>` | Walks from the adapter's own `seeds()` with a small page budget, exactly as a scan would, and prints the discovery as well as the offers. |

The third catches the faults that are not in `parse()` at all: a seed
that 404s, a sitemap index whose first child is 10,000 category pages,
a shop that answers one page and then refuses. Every one of those has
happened to a retailer in this repository.

Save the file and run it again — there is nothing to restart. The
registry is rebuilt whenever anything in `adapters/` changes.

## The interface

```python
class MyBookshop:
    slug = "mybookshop"
    name = "My Bookshop"
    country = "GB"
    domains = ("mybookshop.co.uk", "www.mybookshop.co.uk")
    needs_scraper = False

    def seeds(self): ...
    def parse(self, page): ...
```

| | |
|---|---|
| `slug` | Lowercase, digits and hyphens. Stored on every offer, so renaming it later orphans what this has already found. |
| `name` | What you call the shop. |
| `country` | ISO 3166-1, two capitals. Decides the currency and whether a shelf price is understood to include consumer tax. |
| `domains` | Every hostname this claims. A tuple — a bare string makes each of its letters a hostname, which is why that is refused. Two adapters cannot claim one host. |
| `needs_scraper` | `True` if the shop refuses an ordinary request. Costs you credits on every page, so leave it `False` until you have watched it refuse. |
| `seeds()` | Where a scan starts. Usually one sitemap. |
| `parse(page)` | `page.url`, `page.html`, `page.fetched_at`. Return or yield `Offer`s. |

`parse` gets the HTML and the URL and nothing else: no client, no
credentials, no database. That is not tidiness — it is what makes
running your own code here a reasonable thing to do, and it is enforced
by what `Page` does not carry.

### Optional, and read if present

| | |
|---|---|
| `wants_sitemap(url) -> bool` | Which sitemaps are worth opening. A large shop's index is mostly images, categories and editorial; without this a pass can spend thousands of pages on documents that cannot hold an offer. |
| `request_delay` | Seconds between requests. Only ever *slower* than the install's setting — an adapter may say a shop needs more room, never that it needs less. |
| `scraper_options` | Extra proxy options the shop needs, e.g. `{"render": "true"}`. Declared rather than switched on hopefully, because each one multiplies what a page costs you. |

## A worked example

Medimops sells used books, CDs and DVDs. It is not one of the shipped
retailers, it answers a plain request, and it is conventional in the
way most shops are: the price and the condition are in schema.org
JSON-LD, and the barcode is not.

```python
import re

from biryar.sourcing import Condition, Offer, Page, barcode, schema_org

#: ``ISBN / EAN:`` and its value, from the product-details table.
EAN = re.compile(
    r"ISBN\s*/\s*EAN:\s*</dt>\s*<dd[^>]*>\s*([0-9\s-]+?)\s*</dd>",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)


class Medimops:
    slug = "medimops"
    name = "Medimops"
    country = "DE"
    domains = ("medimops.de", "www.medimops.de")
    needs_scraper = False

    def seeds(self):
        return ["https://www.medimops.de/sitemap_index_deu.xml"]

    def wants_sitemap(self, url: str) -> bool:
        # The index lists 160 children, one of which is categories.
        return "sitemap_product" in url

    def parse(self, page: Page):
        stated = EAN.search(page.html)
        if stated is None:
            return                       # not a product page
        gtin = barcode.read(stated.group(1))
        if not gtin:
            return                       # or not a real barcode

        for node in schema_org.products(schema_org.blocks(page.html)):
            listing = schema_org.first_offer(node)
            price = schema_org.price(listing)
            title = str(node.get("name") or "").strip()
            if not title or price is None:
                continue
            if not schema_org.buyable(listing):
                continue

            yield Offer(
                retailer=self.slug,
                url=page.url,
                title=title,
                sku=gtin,
                price=price,
                currency=str(listing.get("priceCurrency") or "EUR"),
                gtin=gtin,
                brand=schema_org.brand(node),
                image_url=schema_org.first_image(node),
                # Read, not assumed: this shop sells used and new, and
                # says which. Used is its default, because a used copy
                # screened against Amazon's New buy box is a loss
                # wearing a margin.
                condition=schema_org.condition(listing, Condition.USED),
                in_stock=True,
                price_includes_tax=True,     # a German shelf price does
            )
```

Two things in there are worth copying, and one is worth noticing.

The barcode is read from the label, not from the class. The real markup
is

```html
<dt class="ProductAttributes_rowDefinition__8PGYQ">ISBN / EAN:</dt>
<dd class="ProductAttributes_rowValue__fWL3F">9781848125582</dd>
```

and `__8PGYQ` is generated at build time. An adapter keyed on it stops
finding barcodes after the shop's next deploy *without stopping
working*: pages read, offers dropped, no error anywhere. The label is
the part a person maintains, so it is the part to match.

`barcode.read` is used rather than the string itself. A number in a
field called EAN is not an EAN until its check digit says so.

And a missing barcode returns rather than guessing. That is what makes
the adapter safe to point at a whole sitemap: anything that is not a
product page simply yields nothing.

## What an offer has to get right

```python
Offer(
    retailer=self.slug,
    url=page.url,
    title="…",
    sku="…",
    price=Decimal("16.99"),
    currency="GBP",
    gtin="5054061482232",
    condition=Condition.NEW,
    in_stock=True,
    price_includes_tax=True,
)
```

Four of these decide whether a candidate is right, wrong, or quietly
dropped. They are worth more attention than the parsing.

**`gtin` — no barcode, no candidate.** It is the only reliable route to
an Amazon listing; title-and-image matching is slower and wrong more
often, so an offer without one is skipped before a paid lookup is spent
on it. It is also *checked*: a GTIN carries its own check digit, and a
number that fails is treated as no barcode at all. One shipped retailer
publishes its own article number in `gtin13` on about one product in
six, and eight digits is a legal GTIN-8 length, so nothing but the check
digit tells them apart.

**`condition` — the default is `UNSTATED`, and that is not `NEW`.** The
screening step refuses to compare an unstated condition with Amazon's
New buy box, so forgetting this gives you a scan that reads pages, spends
lookups and produces no candidates, with `condition_mismatch` in the run
report to say why. Read it from the page where the page says it. A used
book priced against the New buy box is a loss wearing a margin.

**`price_includes_tax`** — a German or British shelf price does; a United
States one does not. Getting it wrong moves every margin by the VAT
rate, which is why it is stated rather than guessed from the currency.

**`currency`** — read it from the page rather than assuming it from the
country. A British shop has answered this machine in US dollars. Fees
measured in one currency cannot price a listing in another, and the
screening step refuses rather than converting.

## What the shipped retailers learned the hard way

Every one of these came from a real page, and every one of them failed
*quietly* — a healthy 200 and an empty result, never an error.

**Structured data lies about state.** The rule that holds across all
seventeen is *identity from the structured data, state from the page*.
A `Product` block is a contract the shop maintains with search engines;
it is not kept in sync with the shelf. One retailer's JSON-LD gives a
price that has since been marked down and an availability that
contradicts its own buy button. Another's `itemCondition` is a constant
that says `NewCondition` on a shop that sells nothing new. Argos
publishes JSON-LD with no barcode and an availability of `OutOfStock`
for a product its own page state says is in stock and deliverable.

**A dead product URL often answers 200.** HMV serves the parent
category: twenty-five tiles, each with a name, a price and an
availability, none of them the product that was asked for. Read
naively that is twenty-five confident offers at other products' prices.
Find something that is true of a product page and false of a listing —
there, exactly one `<h1 itemprop="name">` and exactly one barcode row —
and yield nothing when it does not hold.

**The first URLs in a sitemap are not a sample.** They are clustered.
One shop's first 10,640 sitemap entries are all category pages; another's
begin with several thousand print-on-demand reprints. Judging a
catalogue, or inventing a filter, from the top of a file is how a scan
quietly loses most of a shop. Sample from the middle.

**Several prices on a page, and the right one is not the first.** A
product page carries recommendations, other editions, bundles. Match the
one that belongs to this page by something the URL states — an id, an
ISBN — and check it against what the page says about itself. On one
shop a recommendation happened to carry the same price as the product,
which would have made "the first price on the page" look correct on
exactly the page it was tested against.

**Read the whole document before believing it is empty.** A page can
publish its product as microdata attributes rather than JSON-LD, inside
a `window.__data` JavaScript object, in `data-` attributes on a buy
button, or in Open Graph meta tags. All four are in this repository
because all four were, at first, mistaken for a shop with nothing on it.

## Where the files live

`adapters/` next to the checkout, or wherever `BIRYAR_ADAPTERS_DIR`
points. Every `*.py` in it is imported when a scan runs; names starting
with `_` are skipped, so notes and half-written things can sit there.

One file is one adapter's worth of code. The directory is deliberately
not on `sys.path`, so an adapter cannot import a sibling file — a
directory on the path shadows standard-library modules by accident, and
a file called `json.py` in there would be a very confusing afternoon.

A file that does not load does not stop the others, and does not go
quiet either: the reason appears on the sourcing screen and in
`python -m biryar.adapters list`, which exits non-zero when anything
failed.

Your adapters are not committed — `.gitignore` excludes `adapters/*.py`,
so updating Biryar will not touch them and they will not arrive in a
pull request. Keep a copy of anything you would be sorry to lose.

## Only on your own machine

Importing a file runs it. On a hosted deployment that means running one
seller's code inside a process that holds every other seller's Amazon
refresh token and an open database connection — and no review of an
adapter's *interface* changes that, because the damage is done at
import, before any method is called.

So the directory is read on a self-hosted install and ignored
everywhere else, and the refusal happens before anything is imported.
Keeping `parse` pure is what leaves a sandboxed third option open
later.
